entry: Top-level professional [[Association football]] league in [[Spain]]. Officially LaLiga EA Sports for sponsorship reasons, it was founded in 1929 as the *Primera División* and is governed by the *Liga Nacional de Fútbol Profesional*. The league has 20 teams, which play a double round-robin schedule of 38 matches each season, from August to May, with three points for a win and one for a draw. The three lowest-placed clubs are relegated to the *Segunda División*, and the top two clubs from that division are promoted, with a third club promoted through play-offs. Real Madrid and Barcelona have dominated the competition, winning 36 and 29 titles, and nine clubs have been crowned champions. Clubs from the league have won 20 [[UEFA Champions League]] titles, more than those of any other league. Average attendance for league matches was 26,933 in the 2018–19 season, the eighth-highest of any domestic professional sports league.

Vengeful ghost in Hispanic American folklore. Said to roam near bodies of water, mourning the children she drowned in a river, she is believed to bring misfortune, death, or extreme failure to anyone who hears her crying. The legend is well known in Mexico and the southwestern United States and is traditionally told throughout Mexico, Central America, and northern South America. She is sometimes conflated with [[La Malinche]]. Three approaches have been proposed to explain its origin: a literal account of events, a myth overlaid on a real story, and a symbolic reading that gives voice to Indigenous peoples during the Conquest and colonization.

Nahua interpreter and advisor to [[Hernán Cortés]]. She was one of 20 enslaved women given to the Spaniards in 1519 by the Amerindians of Tabasco, Mexico, and she spoke both Nahuatl and Maya. She contributed to the Spanish invasion of the [[Aztec Empire]] (1519–1521) as an interpreter, advisor, and intermediary. Cortés chose her as a consort, and she bore him a son, Martín, one of the first [[Mestizo|mestizos]] in New Spain. Historians emphasize her importance to the conquest but disagree about why she assisted the Spanish. After Mexico won independence from Spain in 1821, dramas, novels, and paintings often portrayed her as an evil or scheming temptress. Today she remains a powerful symbol in Mexico, understood as the embodiment of treachery, the quintessential victim, or the symbolic mother of the Mexican people. The term *malinchista* refers to a disloyal compatriot, especially in Mexico.

Seat of government of [[Bolivia]]. Set in a canyon 68 km southeast of [[Lake Titicaca]] at about 3,650 m (11,975 ft) above sea level, it is the highest administrative capital in the world. Founded on 20 October 1548 by Spanish conquistador Alonso de Mendoza, it was named Nuestra Señora de La Paz to commemorate the restoration of peace after an insurrection against the first viceroy of Peru. With 755,732 residents as of 2024, it is the third-most populous city in Bolivia, and its metropolitan area, including El Alto, is the second-most populous urban area. The *Palacio Quemado*, the presidential palace, and the Plurinational Legislative Assembly are in the city, while the judiciary sits in the constitutional capital, Sucre. La Paz generates 24% of the nation's [[Gross domestic product|gross domestic product]] and is home to the largest urban cable car network in the world.

Opera in four acts by [[Giacomo Puccini]]. Composed between 1893 and 1895 to an Italian libretto by Luigi Illica and Giuseppe Giacosa, it is based on Henri Murger's 1851 *Scènes de la vie de bohème* and is set in Paris around 1830. It depicts the Bohemian lifestyle of a poor seamstress, Mimì, and her artist friends, focusing on her relationship with Rodolfo and ending with her death. The world premiere took place on 1 February 1896 at the Teatro Regio in Turin, conducted by the 28-year-old Arturo Toscanini. The opera quickly entered the standard Italian repertory and is among the most frequently performed operas worldwide. In 1946, 50 years after the premiere, Toscanini conducted a commemorative radio performance with the NBC Symphony Orchestra; it is the only recording of a Puccini opera made by its original conductor. The opera influenced adaptations such as the musical [[Rent (musical)|Rent]].

Opera in three acts by [[Giuseppe Verdi]]. Verdi set it to an Italian libretto by Francesco Maria Piave, based on the play *La Dame aux camélias* (1852) by Alexandre Dumas fils, who had adapted it from his own 1848 novel. The opera was originally titled *Violetta*, after its heroine, and premiered on 6 March 1853 at La Fenice opera house in Venice. The authorities at La Fenice insisted that it be set in the past, around 1700, although Verdi and Piave wanted a contemporary setting. Realistic modern-dress productions were not staged until the 1880s, and the opera has since become one of the most frequently performed of all operas.

Major externally visible structures of the [[Vulva]]. In humans and other [[Primate|primates]] there are two pairs. The labia majora (outer lips) are large, thick folds of skin that cover the other vulvar parts, and their outer surface develops pubic hair during puberty. The labia minora (inner lips) are folds of skin between the outer labia that surround and protect the urethral and vaginal openings and the glans of the [[Clitoris|clitoris]]. In other [[Mammal|mammals]], the labia majora are absent and the labia minora are called labia vulvae. The term derives from the Latin *labium*, meaning lip.

Facility providing controlled conditions for scientific or technological research, experiments, and measurement. Laboratories are found in [[University|universities]], schools, corporate and government research centers, forensic investigation centers, hospitals, and clinics, and occasionally in personal residences. Equipment depends on the discipline: a physics laboratory might contain a [[Particle accelerator|particle accelerator]] or vacuum chamber, while a chemist or biologist might use a wet laboratory. The earliest known laboratory was a home laboratory of [[Pythagoras]] of Samos, where he studied the tones of sound and vibrating strings. The first physics laboratory was established in 1833 at Göttingen University, and team research began in the 19th century. Big Science during World War II enlarged laboratories and introduced particle accelerators and similar devices.

Center-left political party in the [[United Kingdom]], historically an alliance of democratic socialists, social democrats, and trade unionists. Founded in 1900, it briefly formed a minority government in 1924 and won a majority in 1945 under [[Clement Attlee]], whose government carried out extensive nationalization, established the National Health Service, and created the modern [[Welfare state|welfare state]]. Under [[Tony Blair]] it moved toward the political center and governed from 1997 to 2007. Keir Starmer led the party to victory in the 2024 general election, and Andy Burnham succeeded him as leader and prime minister in 2026.

Subfield of [[Economics|economics]] concerned with markets for wage labor. It studies labor supply, which varies with age, education, gender, and childbearing, and the demand by firms for different kinds of labor as an input to production. Other topics include schooling and human capital, [[Discrimination|discrimination]], collective bargaining and [[Trade union|trade unions]], technological change and [[Unemployment|unemployment]], and public policies such as unemployment benefits, pensions, health care, and minimum wages. The labor force comprises people of working age who are employed or actively looking for work, and the unemployment rate is unemployment divided by the labor force. Frictional unemployment reflects the time it takes people to find jobs suited to their skills, and technological advancement often reduces it.

British breed of retriever [[Gun dog|gun dog]]. Developed in the United Kingdom from St. John's water dogs imported from the Colony of Newfoundland, it was named after the Labrador region of that colony. Labradors are often friendly, energetic, and playful. Bred as sporting and hunting dogs, they are widely kept as companions and may be trained as guide, assistance, rescue, or therapy dogs. They are intelligent and need both physical and mental stimulation. The Kennel Club recognized the breed in 1903, and the first American Kennel Club registration followed in 1917. Labradors are prone to [[Obesity|obesity]], which can be managed through nutrition and portion control.

Arm of the [[Atlantic Ocean|North Atlantic Ocean]] between the Labrador Peninsula and [[Greenland]]. It connects to [[Baffin Bay]] through the Davis Strait. The sea formed when the North American and Greenland plates separated, a process that began about 60 million years ago and stopped about 40 million years ago. It is about 3,400 m deep where it joins the Atlantic. Water temperatures range from −1 °C (30 °F) in winter to 5–6 °C (41–43 °F) in summer, and two-thirds of the sea is covered in ice during winter. The sea is a major source of North Atlantic Deep Water, a cold water mass, and it contains the Northwest Atlantic Mid-Ocean Channel, one of the world's largest turbidity current channel systems. Icebergs carried by its currents hinder navigation.

Decorative openwork [[Textile|textile]] consisting of a pattern of holes, made by hand or machine. Lace can be formed by techniques such as needle lace, which uses needle and thread, or cutwork, which uses pre-existing fabric. It can be made of any thread, though cotton is widely used; early forms used linen, [[Silk|silk]], gold, or silver thread. Lace is commonly used to embellish clothing and household linens. Its origin is unclear, but the earliest examples are from 16th-century Italy. By the 17th and 18th centuries, lace was integral to high fashion, adorning collars, cuffs, and veils in court attire. Machine production in the 19th century made lace more widely available and diminished the prestige of handmade variants, which persist in niche crafts and couture.

Contact team sport played with a lacrosse stick and ball, and the oldest organized sport in North America. Indigenous peoples of North America played early forms of the game as early as the 12th century, using it for ceremony, to resolve intertribal disputes, and to train warriors. European colonists modified it to reduce violence, creating the collegiate and professional forms played today. Five versions exist: field lacrosse, women's lacrosse, box lacrosse, lacrosse sixes, and intercrosse. Men's field and box lacrosse are contact sports, while women's play allows stick contact but no body contact. Governed by World Lacrosse, the sport holds world championships every four years. Lacrosse was contested at the 1904 and 1908 [[Summer Olympic Games|Summer Olympics]], and it will return at the 2028 Olympics in the sixes format.

Organic acid, C₃H₆O₃, found in [[Milk|milk]]. It is white as a solid and miscible with water. As an alpha-hydroxy acid, it has a hydroxyl group next to its carboxyl group, and its conjugate base is lactate. Lactic acid exists as two mirror-image forms, L- and D-lactic acid. In animals, L-lactate is produced from pyruvate by the enzyme lactate dehydrogenase during normal metabolism and exercise, and it accumulates when production exceeds removal. In industry, lactic acid bacteria convert simple sugars such as [[Glucose|glucose]], sucrose, or galactose into lactic acid, and the acid these bacteria produce in the mouth causes [[Tooth decay|tooth decay]]. Swedish chemist Carl Wilhelm Scheele first isolated it from sour milk in 1780. Lactate is one of the main components of lactated Ringer's solution, used for fluid resuscitation after blood loss.

Disaccharide of galactose and glucose, found in [[Milk|milk]]. It makes up around 2–8% of milk by mass and is the predominant sugar in the milk of most mammals. Its name comes from *lac*, the Latin word for milk. Bovine milk contains about 4.8% lactose. Industrially, lactose is extracted from whey, the liquid left after milk is curdled for [[Cheese|cheese]] production, and it is used in pharmaceuticals, food additives, and infant formula. In the small intestine, the enzyme lactase splits lactose into [[Glucose|glucose]] and galactose. In most mammals, lactase production gradually declines after weaning, and people who cannot digest lactose may experience diarrhea, bloating, and flatulence. More than 70% of western Europeans digest lactose as adults, compared with less than 30% of people from areas of Africa, eastern and southeastern Asia, and Oceania.

Vertical or steeply inclined set of rungs or steps used for climbing or descending. Rigid ladders are self-supporting or leaned against a wall, and most are portable, though some are permanently fixed to a structure. Flexible ladders, such as those of [[Rope|rope]] or wire, hang from the top. Ladders are ancient: a [[Mesolithic]] rock painting in the Spider Caves near [[Valencia]], Spain, shows a person using a long, flexible ladder to harvest honey. Many specialized types exist, including extension ladders, folding stepladders, and roof ladders with a hook that grips a ridge. Ladders remain indispensable in construction, maintenance, firefighting, and household use, though falls from them cause thousands of injuries each year.

American singer, songwriter, and actress. She has an estimated 124 million records in sales, making her one of the best-selling music artists of all time. Her debut album, *The Fame* (2008), was followed by *Born This Way* (2011), and she later released albums in electronic dance, jazz, and soft rock styles. She starred in *A Star Is Born* (2018) and *House of Gucci* (2021). Her contributions to the *A Star Is Born* soundtrack made her the first person to win an Academy, BAFTA, Golden Globe, and [[Grammy Awards|Grammy Award]] in one year. Her philanthropy focuses on mental health awareness and LGBTQ rights.

Order of [[Mammal|mammals]] comprising rabbits, hares, and pikas. Lagomorphs are closely related to [[Rodent|rodents]], from which they differ in having four upper incisors instead of two. Both groups have continuously growing incisors that must be worn down by chewing fibrous food. Lagomorphs have more cheek teeth than rodents and are almost exclusively herbivores. The order has two living families: Leporidae, which includes rabbits and hares, and Ochotonidae, the pikas. Its 110 recent species live on every continent except Antarctica. The name, from Ancient Greek for hare and form, was coined in 1855 by Johann Friedrich von Brandt, and the order was formally described in 1912. Fossil records indicate that many more species lived in the past.

Shallow body of water separated from a larger body of water by a narrow landform. Lagoons are commonly divided into coastal lagoons, also called barrier lagoons, and [[Atoll|atoll]] lagoons, which are enclosed by coral reefs. Coastal lagoons are separated from the sea by a reef, barrier island, barrier peninsula, or [[Isthmus|isthmus]], and they often overlap with [[Estuary|estuaries]]. Coastal lagoons are usually less than 2 m deep and often brackish, while atoll lagoons tend to be deeper and fully saline. In coral reef science the term is synonymous with back reef. The word comes from the Venetian *laguna*, which refers to the waters around [[Venice]] and derives from Latin *lacus*, meaning lake.

Method in [[Mathematical optimization|mathematical optimization]] for finding the local maxima and minima of a function subject to equation constraints. Named after [[Joseph-Louis Lagrange]], it converts a constrained problem into an unconstrained one through a Lagrangian function, which combines the objective with each constraint weighted by a multiplier λ. The solutions are stationary points of this function, where all partial derivatives, including those with respect to λ, are zero. The solution is always a saddle point of the Lagrangian. The method avoids explicit parameterization of the constraints, and the Karush–Kuhn–Tucker conditions generalize it to inequality constraints.

Equilibrium point for a small object under the gravitational influence of two massive orbiting bodies. Five such points exist for any pair of bodies, labeled L1 through L5 and lying in their orbital plane. At these points the gravitational forces of the two bodies balance the centrifugal pseudo-force, so satellites there need minimal fuel to hold position. L1, L2, and L3 lie on the line joining the bodies, while L4 and L5 form equilateral triangles with them. [[Leonhard Euler]] discovered the three collinear points, and [[Joseph-Louis Lagrange]] found the other two. L4 and L5 are stable when the mass ratio is large enough, and Jupiter has more than one million trojan [[Asteroid|asteroids]] near them. The [[James Webb Space Telescope]] is located at the Sun–Earth L2 point.

Formulation of [[Classical mechanics|classical mechanics]] founded on the d'Alembert principle of virtual work. Introduced by [[Joseph-Louis Lagrange]] in 1760 and presented in his 1788 work *Mécanique analytique*, it describes a system by its configuration space and a Lagrangian, which for many systems is the kinetic energy minus the potential energy. The stationary action principle requires the action derived from the Lagrangian to be stationary along the path the system follows, and Lagrange's equations yield the equations of motion. Unlike Newtonian mechanics, which starts from forces, the approach uses energy and generalized coordinates, which avoids calculating constraint forces directly. Its influence extends to relativity and [[Quantum field theory|quantum field theory]], and symmetries in the Lagrangian yield conserved quantities through [[Noether's theorem]].

Capital and largest city of the Pakistani province of [[Punjab]]. It is the second-largest city in Pakistan, after [[Karachi]], and a major industrial, educational, and economic hub. The site has been inhabited for over two millennia, and Lahore rose to prominence in the late 10th century. It served as the capital of several empires, including the Ghaznavid Empire and Delhi Sultanate, and was one of the principal cities of the [[Mughal Empire]], serving as its capital under Akbar. Lahore declined in the 18th century before becoming capital of the Sikh Kingdom of Lahore in the early 19th century. The East India Company annexed it in 1849, and the city was central to the independence movements of British India. The Lahore Fort and Shalimar Gardens are [[UNESCO]] World Heritage Sites.

Soviet space dog and the first animal to orbit Earth. A stray mongrel from the streets of Moscow, she was launched aboard Sputnik 2 on 3 November 1957. Her survival was never expected, because technology to re-enter the atmosphere had not been developed. She died hours into the flight from overheating. The true cause and time of her death were not made public until 2002, and the Soviet government initially claimed she was euthanized. [[Nikita Khrushchev]] wanted a spacecraft launched to mark the 40th anniversary of the [[October Revolution]], and [[Sergei Korolev]] proposed a dog as its passenger.
